meta.title: Federal Criminal Common Law Atlas
meta.data_status: Headline and acknowledgment distributions are final under the stated protocol. Mode, hook, and source-use detail remains provisional because smaller disputes were not adjudicated.
meta.citation_status: The in-corpus citation graph is a regex-derived floor, not a complete citator.

prompt_sensitivity.note: Same-model shadow audit. The unqualified run was quarantined and never entered the headline.

limitations: This is a census of the constructed Supreme Court corpus, not a sample from all possible judicial behavior; comparisons are descriptive, not causal.

The 460-case binary headline and acknowledgment distribution are final under the protocol. Ninety-nine mode-granularity, eighty-nine hook, and several source-use disputes remain intentionally unresolved.
Modes and acknowledgments are nonexclusive, so their category counts can exceed the number of cases.
Opinion citations are a regex-derived floor; Hudson analysis additionally uses commercial citator reports and a full-text audit because older reports mix opinions and counsel arguments.

method.scope_note: Commercial citator lists disagree and older U.S. Reports print counsel arguments alongside opinions. The Atlas therefore separates raw citator records from locally verified judicial contexts and preserves supplemental full-text hits.
method.semantic_note: Role labels are nonexclusive, keyword-assisted research tags. The cited passages and the load-bearing historical examples were reviewed; the tags are navigational, not precedential-treatment codes.

phases.title: A contested jurisdictional settlement
phases.description: Coolidge preserved Hudson without reconsidering it, and Ortega still described the question as open to reargument. The rule existed before it hardened into canonical statutory-grounding language.

phases.title: From jurisdictional holding to statutory-grounding canon
phases.description: Reese, Britton, Eaton, Gradwell, and Flores used Hudson to insist on statutory authorization, while other cases mined the opinion for jurisdiction and contempt principles.

phases.title: A broader federal-lawmaking limit
phases.description: After Erie, opinions began pairing Hudson with wider limits on federal judicial lawmaking. At the same time, Morissette and related criminal cases invoked the statutory-only premise while supplying general-part rules through interpretation.
milestones: D'Oench, Duhme & Co. v. Federal Deposit Insurance
United States v. Standard Oil Co. Of California

phases.title: Orthodoxy, analogy, and the opinion's exception
phases.description: Milwaukee and Parratt made Hudson an Erie-like general-common-law citation; Liparota, Dowling, and Staples restated federal crimes as statutory creatures; Chambers and related cases emphasized Hudson's inherent-powers passage.

phases.title: Separation of powers and democratic legality
phases.description: Modern opinions deploy Hudson against judicial crime definition, vague statutes, criminal-law deference, and aggressive construction, while the jurisdictional and inherent-powers strands remain available outside criminal law.
milestones: United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers' Cooperative
